name: Immigrants Rising Entrepreneurship Fund
description: The Immigrants Rising Entrepreneurship Fund provides microgrants and technical assistance to undocumented immigrant entrepreneurs in the United States. The fund supports individuals who are building businesses that create positive social change in their communities. Grantees receive seed capital along with access to business development workshops, mentorship from experienced entrepreneurs, and peer networking opportunities. Since receiving a $5.41 million California SEED Grant, Immigrants Rising has disbursed over $4 million in microgrants and technical assistance to more than 650 immigrant entrepreneurs across California. The fund is open to undocumented individuals, DACA recipients, and those with Temporary Protected Status (TPS) who face significant barriers to traditional business financing.
eligibility: Undocumented immigrants, DACA recipients, and Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders residing in the United States; must be developing or operating a business with a social impact component; no Social Security number required
applicationProcess: Visit immigrantsrising.org and navigate to the Entrepreneurship Fund page. Applications open periodically — sign up for email notifications to be alerted when the next cycle opens. Submit a business plan or description, personal statement, and budget proposal. Selected applicants may be invited for an interview. Contact the Entrepreneurship Team at [email protected] for questions.
geographicScope: United States — primarily California, with some national opportunities
documentsRequired: Business plan or description, personal statement, proposed budget, proof of ITIN or other identification, evidence of business activity or concept

name: NASE Growth Grants for Self-Employed Entrepreneurs
description: The National Association for the Self-Employed (NASE) awards Growth Grants of up to $4,000 quarterly to help micro-business owners and self-employed individuals grow their businesses. Four winners are chosen each quarter, making this a recurring opportunity throughout the year. Since 2006, NASE has awarded nearly $1 million in growth grants. Grants can be used for marketing, advertising, hiring employees, expanding facilities, purchasing equipment, and other specific business needs. This program is particularly valuable for immigrant entrepreneurs who are NASE members, as it does not require citizenship or specific immigration status — only current NASE membership in good standing. NASE membership also provides access to health insurance options, tax advice, and business education resources.
eligibility: Must be a current NASE member in good standing; annual members may apply immediately, monthly members may apply 90 days after joining; business must be a micro-business (generally fewer than 10 employees); open to self-employed individuals regardless of immigration status
applicationProcess: Join NASE as a member (annual or monthly plan). After meeting the membership duration requirement, register at apply-nase-gs.smapply.io using your NASE credentials. Complete the Growth Grant application including a business description, growth plan, and how the funds will be used. Applications are reviewed quarterly and four winners are announced each quarter.
documentsRequired: Active NASE membership, business description, growth plan detailing how funds will be used, supporting documentation for business activities

name: SBA Program for Investment in Micro-Entrepreneurs (PRIME)
description: The Program for Investment in Micro-Entrepreneurs (PRIME) is a federal grant program administered by the U.S. Small Business Administration that funds organizations helping disadvantaged micro-entrepreneurs — including immigrants and refugees with limited English proficiency — start and grow small businesses. PRIME grants support technical assistance providers who deliver training, mentoring, and business development services to low-income individuals who lack sufficient education, training, or resources to access traditional capital markets. While PRIME does not provide grants directly to individual entrepreneurs, the funded organizations offer free or low-cost business training, one-on-one mentoring, assistance with business plan development, and help accessing microloans. This is a key pipeline for immigrant entrepreneurs to receive guided support in launching U.S.-based businesses.
eligibility: Low-income individuals, including immigrants and refugees, who lack sufficient training, education, or resources to access traditional business financing; services delivered through PRIME-funded organizations; no specific immigration status requirement for receiving services
amount: Free technical assistance — training, mentoring, and business plan development provided at no cost through funded organizations
applicationProcess: Find a PRIME-funded organization near you through the SBA website or by contacting your local SBA district office. Contact the organization to enroll in their micro-entrepreneur training program. Services typically include business plan development workshops, financial literacy training, marketing guidance, and connections to microloan providers.
geographicScope: United States — through PRIME-funded organizations in various states
documentsRequired: Varies by organization — generally proof of income, identification, and business concept or plan

name: Tory Burch Foundation Fellows Program
description: The Tory Burch Foundation Fellows Program selects 50 women entrepreneurs annually and awards each a $5,000 business education grant plus a year-long fellowship experience. Fellows gain access to the Fellows Lab — an exclusive virtual community for networking, mentorship, and peer support. The program also provides IFundWomen coaching, one-on-one mentoring from successful entrepreneurs, and access to capital resources. Since its inception, the Foundation has awarded over $5 million in grants and helped thousands of women build successful businesses. The program is open to women entrepreneurs across the United States, including immigrant women who are authorized to work, making it a valuable funding and networking opportunity for women newcomers building businesses in the U.S.
eligibility: Women entrepreneurs who own and operate a for-profit business in the United States; business must be at least one year old; must be authorized to work in the U.S.; priority given to women-owned businesses with demonstrated growth potential and community impact
amount: $5,000 business education grant plus fellowship benefits
applicationProcess: Applications open annually — check the Tory Burch Foundation website for current cycle dates. Submit an online application including business overview, financial information, growth strategy, and personal statement. Finalists are reviewed by a selection committee. 50 fellows are chosen each year and notified via email. The fellowship year includes virtual workshops, mentoring sessions, and the Fellows Lab community.
documentsRequired: Business registration documents, financial statements, business plan or growth strategy, personal statement, proof of at least one year of business operations

name: Wilson-Fish Alternative Program — Refugee Economic Self-Sufficiency
organization: Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
description: The Wilson-Fish Alternative Program provides resettled refugees with a comprehensive package of support services aimed at achieving rapid economic self-sufficiency. The program offers temporary cash assistance, employment services, English language training, and critically, small business development support for refugee entrepreneurs. Wilson-Fish programs operate as an alternative to traditional state-administered refugee assistance, often providing more flexible and culturally responsive services. For aspiring refugee entrepreneurs, the program connects them with business training, mentoring, microloan programs, and startup support. Services are delivered through a network of local organizations and resettlement agencies across participating states. The program serves refugees, asylees, Cuban/Haitian entrants, Special Immigrant Visa holders, and victims of trafficking.
eligibility: Refugees, asylees, Cuban/Haitian entrants, Special Immigrant Visa holders, certified victims of trafficking, and certain Amerasians admitted to the United States; must be within the eligibility period for refugee services (typically up to 5 years after arrival)
amount: Temporary cash assistance plus free employment and business development services — amounts vary by state and individual circumstances
applicationProcess: Contact your local refugee resettlement agency or the Office of Refugee Resettlement to determine if your state participates in the Wilson-Fish program. Eligible individuals are typically enrolled through their resettlement agency upon arrival. Services include intake assessment, employment plan development, job placement assistance, and referrals to business development programs.
geographicScope: United States — participating states (not all states operate Wilson-Fish programs)
documentsRequired: Proof of refugee or asylee status (I-94, I-571, asylum approval letter), Social Security card or application receipt, identification document, proof of U.S. residence

name: Canada Startup Visa Program
description: The Canada Startup Visa Program offers permanent residency to immigrant entrepreneurs who can secure support from a designated Canadian venture capital fund, angel investor group, or business incubator. Unlike most countries that only offer temporary visas to startup founders, Canada provides a direct pathway to permanent residency from day one. To qualify, entrepreneurs need a letter of support from a designated organization: at least CA $200,000 from a venture capital fund, CA $75,000 from an angel investor group, or acceptance into a designated business incubator program. The business must be incorporated in Canada with the applicant holding at least 10% voting rights. This program has made Canada one of the most attractive destinations globally for immigrant entrepreneurs, combining business opportunity with immigration stability.
eligibility: Immigrant entrepreneurs from any country with a qualifying business concept; must secure a letter of support from a designated Canadian organization (venture capital fund, angel investor group, or business incubator); must meet language requirements (CLB 5 in English or French); must have sufficient settlement funds; each applicant must hold at least 10% of voting rights in the business
amount: No direct funding — provides permanent residency; investment amounts depend on designated organization (minimum CA $75,000 angel / CA $200,000 VC)
applicationProcess: Develop a qualifying business concept and pitch to designated Canadian organizations (list available on IRCC website). Secure a letter of support from a designated venture capital fund, angel investor group, or business incubator. Submit permanent residence application to IRCC with the letter of support, language test results, proof of settlement funds, and police certificates. Processing times vary but work permits may be issued while PR application is pending.
geographicScope: Canada — business must be incorporated and operated in Canada
documentsRequired: Letter of support from designated organization, language test results (IELTS or TEF), proof of settlement funds, police certificates, medical examination, valid passport, business plan, proof of education

name: Ascendus Microloans for Immigrant Entrepreneurs
description: Ascendus provides microloans ranging from $500 to $100,000 specifically designed for minority and immigrant small business owners who cannot access traditional bank financing. As one of the largest nonprofit microlenders in the United States, Ascendus has disbursed over $300 million in loans since its founding, primarily to Latino, immigrant, and underserved entrepreneurs. The organization accepts ITIN (Individual Taxpayer Identification Number) in place of a Social Security number, making their loans accessible to a broader range of immigrant entrepreneurs. In addition to capital, Ascendus offers free business coaching, financial education workshops, and connections to additional resources. Their lending criteria focus on business viability and character rather than traditional credit scores, making them a critical funding source for immigrants building businesses in the U.S.
eligibility: Small business owners and entrepreneurs, including immigrants; accepts ITIN in place of SSN; business must be operational or have a viable business plan; no minimum credit score required; must demonstrate ability to repay the loan
applicationProcess: Apply online at ascendus.org or contact their office directly. Submit a loan application including business information, financial projections, and personal details. An Ascendus loan officer will review your application, conduct an interview, and assess business viability. Approved borrowers also receive free business coaching to support success. Typical processing time is 2-4 weeks.
geographicScope: United States — primarily Northeast and Mid-Atlantic states (Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island)
documentsRequired: Government-issued ID or ITIN, business registration documents, bank statements (3-6 months), tax returns or financial statements, business plan for startups, proof of business address
